World Solar Challenge

By: Diana Lucas | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We race with the brightest and the best in the Australian Outbacks.

Summary:
Proposal: World Solar Challenge

It started in 1987, a solar powered car race covering through the Australian Outback from Darwin, through Alice Springs, to Adelaide. Thirty years ago, the cars were as basic as you could go carts, bits of car parts strung together; the organisers: hippies, with a passion or as it turns out a vision.

The idea for the competition was from Danish-born adventurer Hans Tholstrup who was the first person to circumnavigate the Australian continent in an open boat. Already in the 1980’s he had become aware
of the necessity to explore sustainable energy as a replacement for the limited available fossil fuel.
Today the World Solar Challenge is the worlds largest most prestigious solar powered car race covering 3, 021 km attracting teams from around the world most of which are fielded by universities or corporations.

T

Further information:
he objective of this bi-annual competition is to promote research on solar-powered cars. In 2013, 40 teams from 23 countries competed in the race. This year 2015 two of the teams come from South Africa and for the first time we have cars worthy of recognition, cars which international car manufactures are looking at sponsoring.

Carte Blanche will be at this challenging week long race, with the two South African teams as they race their way to the finishing line, sleeping rough in the great Australian outback, contending against some of the brightest young minds in the world and solving challenges together that comes with a race of this nature.

From the University of KwaZulu Natal (UKZN) School of Engineering Solar Energy Research Group a group of engineering students, a solar powered vehicle named Ikiwa named after the short spear used by Shaka Zulu and his warriors. This car has a great lineage it’s previous model defeated only by two Japanese World Champions in the Sasol Solar Challenge.

Efficient balancing of power resources and power consumption is the key to success during the race. At any moment in time the optimal driving speed depends on the weather forecast and the remaining capacity of the batteries. The team members in the escort cars will continuously remotely retrieve data from the solar car about its condition and use these data as input for prior developed computer programs to work out the best driving strategy.

From the University of the North West comes the Sirius X25 a car weighin in at 208 kg and has a length of 4.5kms. The team of 10 engineering students who will travel to Australia…are very excited to call themselves pioneers of the future, as racing their sun-powered car in Australia will help create the beginning of a green future and clean travel. This race promotes the ultimate synergy of nature, motion and innovation and will put our team and their creation through the ultimate trial.

Press Release:


Power of the Sun
It’s the quietest motor race in the world, covers over 3 000 kilometres and is powered only by the sun. Recently, the first ever African participants – two South African university teams – challenged over 40 teams from 25 countries as the world’s cutting-edge and aerodynamic solar cars raced through the Australian outback. Carte Blanche joins the teams at the 13th World Solar Challenge to witness technology of the future in action.


Script:


WORLD SOLAR CHALLENGE

V/O 9 sec
Its 40 degrees in the Australian Outback and snaking soundlessly through the long, hot stretches of road are some rather odd looking vehicles)

Link
This is the 13th World Solar Challenge all the way from Darwin to Adelaide where more than 40 teams from 25 countries are hoping that it is lucky 13 for them.

V/O 11 sec
The race, held every two years, began in 1987 there was a world wide oil crisis and Danish adventurer, Hans Tholstrup, decided to start a car race without oil.

Chris Selwood:
Event Director
People were actually getting murdered for a few litres of fuel and in Australia they banned motor racing because of fuel, so Hans Tholstrup and a few of the other old boys sat around and said if we cant go as fast as we can how about we come up with and idea of how far we can go on how little and that was the embryo of the idea.

V/O 30 sec
Today the Solar Challenge attracts a million students from Universities and Colleges around the world. They are here, to race the cars they have designed and built. It’s not just a showcase of talent but a springboard to the future of technology.

And for the first time two African teams will be racing to the finish.

From the University of Kwa Zulu Natal, is the car Hulamin weighing in at 220kg’s; the team leaders Kirsty Veale and Clinton Bemont.

Dr Clinton Bemont
Team Leader
Lecturer Engineering UKZN

Clinton: Solar car racing is all about how much energy you can get and you can only get your energy from the sun, we have really tried to maximise that very efficient motor only uses the energy of a toaster.
But we can drive the car up to 130 km an hour.

Kirsty Veale
Team Leader
Lecturer Engineering UKZN

Kirsty: The faster you go though the more energy you use the less sun there is the less energy you get in. So the whole time you are driving you’re busy sitting on your calculator of the code you have written to try and drive in the most efficient way.

V/O 9 sec
And from the North West University, Sirius X 25, weighing in at 190 kg’s; team leader Albert Helberg.

Prof. Albert Helberg
Team Manager
Lecturer Electronic Enginering: NWU

Albert: The teams know there is a competitive element with each other but the biggest competition is with your self it is a design competition, so you design a car and you pit it against the most extreme conditions you can find for a solar car.

V/O
Sunday 18th October, is the start of the race, and Darwin’ State Square has become the United Nation of engineers - mechanical, electrical and electronic all testing and fine-tuning their cars. There are three classes, Adventure, Cruiser, and the main class Challenger, the Formula 1 of solar cars.

Derek: This is a sporting event but there is a serious technology side?
Albert: This is like the space programme for solar cars what ever we develop here it ends up in the car.

Chris: One of the things we are very proud of is we have a scientific faculty spend a year coming up with sneaky and cunning ways to make this event harder event by event. It’s not static we have to keep ahead of mainstream technology to push the boundaries.

Link
A few years ago they found that the solar cars were going to fast on the Stuart Highway they were actually breaking the speed limit so what they did was they cut down the allowable size of the solar panel

Chris: Took 25 % of panel away and 2 years later they came back and were back at 100kmph, its actually amazing where that technology goes.

V/O
This is a race as much about aerodynamics as energy management, the solar cars are allowed just 5 kilowatts of stored energy, using no more than six square metres of solar panels which must be fuelled by the sun or kinetic energy for the entire 3000kms,

Siaen : When it started all those years ago you didn’t have the solar cells the batteries to the level they are today so simply by existing it forces people to come together it essentially pushes the industry forward.

V/O
The electronic infra structure in the car, called telemetry, is really the nerve centre, it senses all the variables like temperature, power, speed and transmits them to the follow car.

Bashan Naidoo
Senior Lecturer Electrical Engineering UKZN

We have a control panel where we can observe all the parameters of interest, the power coming from the panel, how much you are using in the motor the status of the battery charge and we can even control certain things from there.

V/O
For the past 15 years the Dutch and Japanese have led the challenge. This year two Dutch teams, Red 1 and Nuna 8 are neck and neck. They have minutes sometimes seconds between each other … so sleeping arrangements can get too close for comfort.

V/O
Whilst Nuna 8 and Red 1 are battling it out for first position, further down the road our teams are having their own race to be the first African team to finish.

Albert:
We see ourselves as friendly rivals so when we on the road we are complete competitors but when we are on the side of the road we have a good chat?

V/O
Old rivals these two teams cut their teeth on South Africa’s Sasol Solar challenge, a race that was started seven years ago.

Kirsty: We took part in the challenge 2012 and designed and built a car in 5 months we did pretty well and we came first in South Africa in our class. Sponsors got very interested they gave us money to take part in the next race in 2014, got so excited wanted to give us the funds to get to Australia.

V/O
So with team Kwazulu Natal having beaten North West in Sasol’s 2014 challenge …. The question is which team will come in ahead now.

V/O
What the South African teams don’t have is the budget, and huge back up of some of the top teams, making pit stops almost five store luxury.

Link
This is evolution from the University of Cambridge it is definitely the most aerodynamic design and its got the most advanced solar cells but they come at a price

Derek: So these are very specialised cells expensive
Yes quiet expensive…in space.

V/O
That’s over 5 million rand for the solar panels alone, about 5 times the budget for the South African teams whole car.

And despite the high price, Cambridge’s super solar car hit technical problems and was trailered off.

The top teams come in a day ahead of time, on Day 5 they start arriving in Adelaide.

LINK
The winners are due here at Victoria Square, it’s been something of a double Dutch challenge, so will it be Nuna 8 or Red 1.

V/O
And it is Nuna 8 who take first prize.

Have you got relatives, sons out there…big YESSSS.

V/O
Red 1 comes in a mere 3 minutes behind Nuna 8.

V/O
And a little later we travel out to meet the teams who are still on the last stretch of the Stuart Highway, The KZN team have just pulled over.

LINK
When it comes to 5 o clock all the teams stop exactly where they are and this is where they will start tomorrow morning at 8 am …

Derek: That was quiet a panic?
Kirsty: We have to get as much sun as possible and tilting it towards the sun every second of sun that we miss is a second of driving we cant do the next day
Derek: Can you still beat Sirius
Maybe…we are the team with many tricks, we did it last year, last year we overtook them on the straight you never know, people think its all about technology and engineering but there is also a lot of luck

V/O
A little further ahead of `KZN 30 kms to be exact North West are settling down for the night after a few final checks on Sirius.

Albert: Its been nerve racking we have been head to head with KZN from Day 1 and today…we have been able to just keep ahead of them all the way, so tomorrow is still race on my nerves are shot.

V/O
The next morning, day 6 the South African teams are due to enter Adelaide.

Link
Well they may be a few hours behind the winners but the crowds are still here to welcome the SA team, We left them last night with Hulamin determined to make up that 30 km gap.

V/O
Its North West who are the first African team to finish the World Solar Challenge,….in 11th place they are in front of major universities like Stanford and MIT.

Arno: We knew the car was reliable we didn’t know the car was that reliable, we hardly touched the car only changed a few tyres.

Albert: I can’t tell you how much this feels like a dream I am still walking in the air

V/O
And Annalie van Vuuren project manager of the Sasol Solar Challenge in South Africa is there to cheer them on.

Annalie: Very excited to have the first South African car competing in the top positions and doing so well, it’s excellent.

V/O
Team KZN come in a little later, in 13th place, for both these teams it’s an extra ordinary achievement.

Shuvay Singh
Driver
Msc Engineering student UKZN

I never dreamt I would do something as incredible as this to think we have crossed the entire continent in just over 5 days.
How does this tie in with your masters?
This was this was my final year project, we designed everything from the bottom up, this isn’t possible without a team you can get a bunch of professionals together and if you don’t have that chemistry and team spirit its never going to work out.
Bashun Naidoo
It is a massive undertaking, such a small budget, across a continent, for me getting ahead of MIT or Cambridge is a big deal.
As you say you have beaten some major universities?
Yes it’s a testament to the std of engineering in SA and engineering education as well.

At any moment in time the optimal driving speed depends on the weather forecast and the remaining capacity of the batteries. The team members in the escort cars will continuously remotely retrieve data from the solar car about its condition and use these data as input for prior developed computer programs to work out the best driving strategy. From the University of the North West comes the Sirius X25 a car weighin in at 208 kg and has a length of 4.5kms. The team of 10 engineering students who will travel to Australia…are very excited to call themselves pioneers of the future, as racing their sun-powered car in Australia will help create the beginning of a green future and clean travel. This race promotes the ultimate synergy of nature, motion and innovation and will put our team and their creation through the ultimate trial.
